paragraphs: The castle my personal servant had dared to break into, rather than let me spend the night outdoors in my desperately wounded state, was one of those great buildings, mixing gloom and grandeur, that have so long frowned among the Appennines—in reality as well as in Mrs. Radcliffe’s imagination. It seemed to have been abandoned only recently, and only for a time. We settled in one of its smallest and least lavishly furnished rooms, in a distant turret. Its decorations were rich, but old and tattered. Tapestries hung on the walls, along with many displays of armour in various forms, and an unusually large number of vivid modern paintings in richly gilded frames with intricate, flowing patterns. These paintings hung not only on the broad walls but in the many recesses created by the castle’s strange architecture. Perhaps the delirium beginning to take hold of me made me so deeply interested in them. I told Pedro to close the room’s heavy shutters, since night had already fallen, light the candles in the tall candelabrum at the head of my bed, and pull wide open the fringed black velvet curtains surrounding the bed itself. I wanted all this done so that, if I could not sleep, I could at least alternate between studying the pictures and reading a small book found on the pillow, which claimed to describe and assess them.

For a long, long time I read, and gazed with deep, devoted attention. The hours flew swiftly and gloriously by until deep midnight came. I disliked the position of the candelabrum. Rather than disturb my sleeping servant, I reached out with difficulty and moved it so that its light fell more fully on the book.

But this produced an entirely unexpected effect. The light of the candles—and there were many—now reached a recess that one of the bedposts had previously kept in deep shadow. There, brightly lit, I saw a picture I had not noticed before. It was a portrait of a young girl just growing into womanhood. I glanced quickly at the painting, then closed my eyes. At first, even I did not understand why I had done so. But while my eyes remained shut, I considered my reason. It had been an instinctive movement to give myself time to think, to make sure my sight had not deceived me, and to calm and control my imagination before looking again more soberly and certainly. After a few moments, I opened my eyes and stared steadily at the painting.

I could not and would not doubt that I now saw it correctly. The first flash of candlelight on the canvas had seemed to scatter the dreamy stupor creeping over my senses and startle me instantly into wakefulness.

As I have said, the portrait was of a young girl. It showed only her head and shoulders, painted in the style technically called a vignette, much like Sully’s popular portraits of heads. Her arms, her breast, and even the ends of her radiant hair melted almost imperceptibly into the indistinct but deep shadow of the background. The frame was oval, richly gilded, with delicate ornament in the Moorish style. As a work of art, the painting could not have been more admirable. Yet neither its craftsmanship nor the face’s immortal beauty could have moved me so suddenly and powerfully. Least of all could my imagination, shaken out of its half-sleep, have mistaken the painted head for a living person’s. I saw at once that the design, the fading edges of the vignette, and the frame must have instantly dispelled such an idea—must have prevented me from entertaining it even for a moment. Thinking hard about these points, I remained half sitting, half reclining, my eyes fixed on the portrait, for perhaps an hour. At last, satisfied that I understood the true secret of its effect, I fell back into bed. I had found the picture’s spell in the absolute lifelikeness of its expression. This had first startled me, then bewildered, overpowered and horrified me. With deep, reverent awe, I returned the candelabrum to its former position. Now that the cause of my agitation was hidden from sight, I eagerly reached for the book about the paintings and their histories. Turning to the number assigned to the oval portrait, I read the following strange, old-fashioned and indistinct words:

“She was a young woman of the rarest beauty, and as full of joy as she was lovely. It was an evil hour when she saw, loved and married the painter. He was passionate, studious and stern, already married to his Art. She was a young woman of the rarest beauty, and as full of joy as she was lovely—all light and smiles, playful as a young fawn, loving and cherishing everything. She hated only Art, her rival, and feared only the palette, brushes and other unwelcome tools that took her lover’s attention from her. It was therefore terrible for her to hear the painter say that he wanted to paint even his young bride. But she was humble and obedient. For many weeks she sat meekly in the dark, high turret room, where light dripped onto the pale canvas only from above. The painter gloried in his work, hour after hour and day after day. He was a passionate, wild and moody man who lost himself in dreams. He would not see that the light falling so ghastly in that lonely turret was withering his bride’s health and spirits. Everyone but him could see her wasting away. Still she smiled and smiled without complaint. She saw that the painter, who was highly renowned, took a feverish, burning pleasure in his task. He worked day and night to paint the woman who loved him so much, yet grew weaker and more dispirited every day. Indeed, some who saw the portrait spoke softly of its likeness, as though it were a mighty marvel. It proved the painter’s power, they said, and just as much his deep love for the woman he painted so superbly. At last, as the work neared its end, no one was allowed into the turret. The painter had grown wild with devotion to his work and rarely took his eyes from the canvas, even to look at his wife’s face. He would not see that the colours he spread on the canvas were drawn from the cheeks of the woman sitting beside him. After many weeks, almost nothing remained to be done: only one stroke on the mouth and one touch of colour in the eye. The lady’s spirit flared once more, like the flame in the socket of a lamp. Then the brushstroke was made, and then the colour was placed. For one moment the painter stood entranced before his work. In the next, still gazing at it, he began to tremble and grew very pale and horrified. Crying aloud, ‘This is indeed Life itself!’ he suddenly turned to look at his beloved:—She was dead!”
